# Path

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How did income and life expectancy change together in each country, year by
year? `path` draws one stroke through the rows' points, *in the order the table
gives them*. That is the whole definition of the mark, and it is the one thing
`line` does not do. A
line sorts its vertices along its domain first, because a line is read as a
*function*: one value for each place on the domain. If two rows have the same
`x`, such as two readings in one year, and no `color` or `group` splits them
into separate lines, the line still joins both: it runs straight up or down at
that `x`, and gog prints a warning, as the plots below show. With two numbers the domain is `x`, so the line is read from left
to right. A path draws a *route*. It
visits row 1, then row 2, and it may turn back, cross itself, or return to where
it started.

The `gapminder_asia` table holds five Asian countries, each measured every five
years from 1952 to 2007, twelve times in all. So every year has five rows, one
for each country, and the table lists China's twelve rows first, then India's.
The top plots draw a line and the bottom plots a path, without and with
`group(country)`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
#| message: true
((data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) +
    title("line, no group")) |
   (data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
      title("line + group(country)"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("path, no group")) |
     (data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
        title("path + group(country)"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 800)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life, beside the same grouped by
country; above a path, x is year, y is life, beside the same grouped by
country."*

On the top left, nothing splits the rows, so the line sorts them by year and
joins the five values of each year. It runs straight up and down at every year,
and gog prints the warning above the plot. On the bottom left, the path keeps
the table's order: it draws China from 1952 to 2007, then jumps back to India in
1952, and so on, so four long lines run back to the left. gog prints no warning,
because following the rows' order is what a path is for. On the right,
`group(country)` gives each country its own stroke. Each country's rows are
already in year order, so the line and the path draw the same picture.

The two marks draw the same kind of stroke. They take the same splits by
`color`, `group` and a mapped `pattern`, and the same `style(size = )` and
`style(pattern = )` settings.
One question separates them: does the order of the rows mean something? A path
keeps that order, and three things follow from it. It can carry an
[arrowhead](#which-end-is-the-last-row), because its last vertex is the table's
last row. [In polar](#a-path-in-polar) it can go around the circle more than
once, because two rows with the same angle stay apart, each on its own turn. And
it can [run through the cube](#a-path-in-the-cube), because the row order does
not depend on any axis. None of the three needs a rule of its own, and each has
a section with a plot later in this chapter.

## The connected scatterplot {#the-connected-scatterplot}

The plots above put the year on `x` and show one measure, life expectancy. To see
how income and life expectancy changed together, put income on `x` and life
expectancy on `y`. No axis is left for the year, but each country's rows are
already in year order. Check the order before you draw any path. A path joins
the rows exactly as the table lists them and never sorts them, so rows in the
wrong order draw a route that never happened. If they are not in order, sort the
table first, in your own language, by the column the route should follow, here
`year`. A path joins these rows in year order, so it still shows time:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country."*

Each route is one country's history. The plot has no time axis, but it still
shows time: time is the order in which the points are joined. China's
route goes almost straight up at very low income. That shape belongs to a
country whose life expectancy rose long before its income did, and India's and
Indonesia's routes rise the same way. Korea's route starts upward and then turns
a sharp corner to the right. Past that corner its income climbs fast and its
life expectancy rises more slowly. Japan's route is the flattest of the five. It
begins where Korea's route turns: Japan had that income and life expectancy in
1952, twenty years before Korea. This is a **connected scatterplot**, and `path`
is the only mark that draws it.

A connected scatterplot usually also draws a dot at each measurement, as a
scatterplot does. The plot above leaves the dots out, so the routes are easier
to follow. Add a `point` layer, colored the same way, and each of the twelve
measurements gets a dot. `style(size = 3)` draws the dots a little smaller than
the default, so they do not crowd the routes at the bottom left:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  point + color(country) + style(size = 3) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same routes, with a point at each measurement")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, colored by country, and also
points colored by country, with size 3."*

The dots are five years apart, so their spacing shows how fast a country
changed. Japan's dots are far apart from the 1960s on, when its income grew
fastest, and China's are close together at the bottom, where its income barely
moved.

## What `line` draws instead {#what-line-draws-instead}

`line` is the mark you would probably write first, because it is the familiar
way to join rows with a stroke. So compare what `line` draws from the same
table. One word changes in the sentence, and two of the five routes visibly
change shape:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("the same data, sorted by x")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is gdp, y is life, color by country."*

Look at Indonesia's route. Its income did not rise steadily: it fell three
times, in 1962, in 1967 and in 2002. So the year order and the income order
differ, and `line` joins the points in income order. Near the bottom of the
plot, Indonesia's line now goes up to its 1967 point, back down to its 1957
point, and up again. Near the top of its route, the fall in 2002 makes a second
zigzag. Every point is still in the right place, but the stroke between them no
longer follows the years. Japan's income fell once, in 2002, and its route
changes the same way near its right end. China's income also fell once, in
1962, by less than 100 dollars. On an axis that runs past 30,000 dollars,
China's points from 1952 to 1967 lie almost in one vertical line, so its route
looks the same in both plots. India's and Korea's income rose at every measurement, so
for them both marks draw the same picture. This is not a defect
in `line`. A line is read as a function, with one value for each `x`, and these
rows have one value for each `x`. Sorting the rows by `x` cannot change which
value belongs to which `x`. For a
time series read along a date axis, the sort simply puts the rows in date order.

The two marks answer different questions. Both sentences are legal, so gog
draws either plot and prints no message. Choosing the mark is your decision
([Law 8](../design-laws.qmd#law-8-pronounceable-usable)), and one rule helps you
make it. If the reader should follow the points in any order other than left to
right, that order has to come from the table, and only `path` takes its order
from the table.

The **bump chart**, which follows each country's rank from year to year, needs
a `path` for another reason. Its `y` is the rank, stored as text (`1st`, `2nd`
and so on), so `y` is a categorical axis. A `line` with a categorical `y` runs
down that axis: it joins each country's points from the top rank to the bottom,
not from the first year to the last. A `path` joins them in the table's order,
which is year order. The `gm_twelve` table holds the ranks in life expectancy of
twelve Asian countries in each of twelve years. It lists all twelve countries
for 1952, then all twelve for 1957, and so on. That order matters for the path:
`color(country)` splits the rows into one path per country, and within each
country the rows come in year order, so each path runs from 1952 to 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_twelve)
```

```{r}
#| message: true
((data(gm_twelve) + x(year) + y(rank) + color(country) + line + point +
    title("line: joined in rank order")) |
   (data(gm_twelve) + x(year) + y(rank) + color(country) + path + point +
      title("path: joined in year order"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 480)
```

*"Given the gapminder twelve: x is year, y is rank, color by country, lines and
also points, beside the same with paths."*

On the left, each country's line joins its ranks from the top down, so a country
whose rank changed draws long strokes back and forth across the years, and gog
prints a message that suggests `path`. On the right, each country moves from
year to year, and a change of rank shows as a step up or down. [Comparing
categories](../cookbook/comparing.qmd#how-did-the-order-change-over-the-years)
draws the bump chart in full.

To put a table in the order a path needs, sort its rows by the column that
splits the paths, then by the column the route follows. For `gm_twelve` that is
`country`, then `year`. This table needs no sorting, because only the order
within each country counts, but a table you read from a file may be in any
order.

## Which end is the last row? {#which-end-is-the-last-row}

A route has a direction, and a plain stroke does not show it. Japan's route
could be read from either end. So `path` takes a setting that a line cannot:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("style(arrow = \"end\"): the head is at 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow
end."*

Now each route points at its last row. `arrow` takes `"end"`, `"start"`, or
`"both"`: an arrowhead (a *head*, for short) at the last row, at the first row,
or at both ends.

Two marks take it: `path`, and [`edge`](edge.qmd), the line between two nodes
of a network. Every other mark refuses it. A line's last vertex
is the row with the largest `x`, so a head there would point at the end of the
sort, not at the last row. A path's end comes from the data. So a line with
`style(arrow = "end")` is refused:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "end")
```

Here `x` is the year, and each country's rows are already in year order. So for
each country's line the sort and the table order agree, and each head would land
on 2007. gog refuses it anyway, because on a line the end of the stroke always
comes from the sort.

## An arrow is a layer {#an-arrow-is-a-layer}

`arrow` has a second use: an arrow from a note to the point it is about. A note placed in an empty
part of the plot has to say which point it is about. An arrow from the words to
the point says it. The [Text](text.qmd#a-note-is-a-layer) chapter drew a note by
itself; here `path` adds the arrow beside one. A note is a one-row table; the
arrow that points from the note to the point it is about is a *two-row* table,
one row for each end.

The plot below adds a note about Botswana to a scatterplot of 2007.
`gapminder_2007` holds one row for each of 142 countries, measured in 2007.
`botswana_arrow` holds the arrow's two ends: row 1 near the note, and row 2
beside Botswana's dot. `botswana_label` holds the note, one row with its place
and its words:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
peek(botswana_arrow)
peek(botswana_label)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(botswana_arrow)  + path + style(arrow = "end", color = "#c0392b") +
  data(botswana_label) + text + label(what) +
  title("an annotation, in the grammar you already have")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also a path from the
Botswana arrow, and text from the Botswana label, label by what."*

`"end"` puts the head on the last row of the arrow's table. In `botswana_arrow`
that is row 2, beside Botswana's dot, so the arrow points from the note to the
dot. With the two rows in the other order, the head would point at the note.

This grammar has no separate function for notes, such as ggplot2's
`annotate()`. An annotation, a
note with its arrow, is made of layers, each over a small table. Its marks are
the marks everything else uses: `text` for the words, `path` for the arrow, and
`point` for a dot at a place you choose. The arrow's
table holds data, so gog scales it like any other table. That is why the
arrow's ends are written in the data's own units rather than in pixels.

On a scatterplot drawn with `point`, there is another way to label a point,
though you cannot set how the label looks. Add `brush()` to the sentence, and on
a web page a click on a point stamps it: a card with the point's values stays
beside it, joined to it by a short line. Drag the card away from the crowded
points, and the line ends in an arrowhead at the point, much like the arrow
above. [Stamping a point](../selection.qmd#stamping-a-point) shows how. A stamp
is gone when the page reloads, but the camera button saves the plot with its
stamps as a picture file. A note drawn with `text` and `path` is part of the
sentence, so it is drawn again every time, for anyone who has the data.

## Two transforms, and the rest refused {#two-transforms-and-the-rest-refused}

Every path so far has been drawn directly from the rows. The next question is
what happens when a transform changes the rows before the path draws them.
`line`, `step`, `area` and `ribbon` compose with many transforms. `path`
composes with two, `density` and [`cluster`](../cluster.qmd), and refuses every
other transform. The summaries show the reason most clearly. [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows `path * mean` being refused.

A summary replaces the rows. `mean` reduces each country to one number, so what
is left to connect is one point per country. Those points are in the order of the
keys (here, the countries), not in the order of the table's rows.
One point per country, joined left to right, is what `line`
already draws. A path's meaning is the row order, and a summary discards that
order. That is why this mark refuses almost every transform, and why its row on
the [Combinations](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-transforms) grid is nearly
empty.

This chapter shows `density` in detail. It draws `cluster` once, in [Transforms
it takes](#transforms-it-takes), and [Cluster](../cluster.qmd) explains it in
full. Like a summary, `density` replaces the rows. Unlike a summary,
its new rows have an order that means something: they are the points around
each ring, in the order the ring is traced.

## The contour: `path * density` {#the-contour-path-density}

Where are the flowers most crowded, and how tightly? The `iris_flowers` table
holds 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species: setosa, versicolor and
virginica. Each row gives one flower's sepal length, sepal width and petal
length, measured in centimeters. A scatterplot of the 150 flowers shows two
groups:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
  title("the 150 flowers as points")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is petal length."*

The small group at the bottom is setosa, whose petals are at most 1.9
centimeters long, and the large group holds the other two species. The 150
flowers lie on only 123 positions, so where several share a position their dots
are drawn on top of each other, and you cannot tell how many are there. A
contour plot leaves the dots out and draws closed rings around the places where
they are most crowded. Bind both positions and compose `density`. gog estimates
the density of points at every place on the plane, then traces the rings on
which that density is the same:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + path * density +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
  title("where the flowers cluster")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density, x is sepal length, y is
petal length."*

The rings are colored from pale to dark, and a legend titled Level gives their
values, although the sentence binds no `color`. `density` gives each ring a
level, the density along it, and gog colors the rings by that level.
[The parameters](#the-parameters) explains the level and shows how to bind
`color` yourself.

Over two positions a density is a **field**: one estimated value at every place
on the plane. Three marks read that field, and each one draws it
differently:

| Mark derived by `density`, over two positions | Shape |
|---|---|
| `zone * density` | the field as filled cells |
| `surface * density` | the field as a sheet in the cube |
| `path * density` | the field as contour rings, the shape this section draws |

The contour above draws that field as rings. The two plots below draw it from
the same table as cells and as a sheet:

```{r}
((data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
    title("zone * density")) |
   (data(iris_flowers) + surface * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
      space() + title("surface * density"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal
length, beside a surface derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal
length, in the cube."*

The zones color each small cell by the density there, and the surface lifts the
same values into two peaks, the two places the contour's rings surround. The
surface needs `space()`, because a sheet lives in the cube. `density` supplies its
height, the density at each place, so the sentence binds only `x` and `y`.
Without `space()`, gog refuses the surface. On
the web page you can turn the cube with the pointer. [Surface](surface.qmd) draws
each one larger and explains them.

That contour needed nothing new in the grammar. One rule produced it, and the
same rule makes `zone * bin` draw a [heatmap](zone.qmd). The rule is that the
mark decides how many positions a transform reads. For `density`, that is the
number of positions it is estimated over, and you never state it yourself. A bar
shows the density as its length, and that length takes one axis. So
`bar * density` estimates the density along the other axis, and draws one thin
bar at each point where it was estimated. A path traces the density's contours,
and a contour needs both axes, so `path * density` estimates the density over
both. So there is no `contour` atom: a contour is written as `path * density`.

Each ring is traced at one value of the density, called its **level**. Read the
outermost ring, then the ones inside it. The outermost is a *single*
ring around both groups, and the next level inward splits into two separate
rings. One level can therefore be several separate rings. So a level is not one
stroke, the way one `color` value is one line. Each ring is drawn as its own
stroke, and the level decides only its color. The two rings of one level are
never joined across the gap between them.

### The parameters {#the-parameters}

The rings are colored by their level, and you did not bind `color` to get that.
Just as `bin` writes a column named `count`, `density` writes a new column,
`level`, into the rows it returns. Each ring's
`level` is the estimated density, which is the same at every place on that
ring, and those are the numbers on the legend. In the plot above they run from about 0.02, for the palest and
outermost ring, to about 0.14 for the darkest. gog bound `color` to `level`, the
same way `bar * bin` binds `y` for you. Bind it yourself if you prefer, and
change how many rings are traced:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + color(level) +
  title("ten levels, named out loud")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 10 levels, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, color by level."*

The rings now come in ten levels instead of the default six, so they are closer
together.

`density` is one transform, and the mark decides what it computes. With `line`
it computes a curve over one column. With `zone` or `path` it computes a field
over two columns: a zone fills the field, and a path draws its rings. The
parameters follow from this. A width suits the curve, and a number of levels
suits the field.

`levels` sets how many levels the contour is traced at, as `levels = 10` did
above. Of the three marks that read the field, `zone` and `path` accept it, and
`surface` refuses it, for a reason [Surface](surface.qmd) gives. `line * density`
refuses it too. Over one column, the density is drawn as a single curve. A
curve has no contour, so there are no levels to count:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(levels = 4) + x(life)
```

To estimate a density, `density` places a small bell-shaped curve on each row
and adds the curves up. `bandwidth` is the width of each of those curves, written
in the column's own units: `bandwidth = 1` on `life` makes each one a year wide
([Choosing the bandwidth](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bandwidth)). A contour
is estimated over two columns, and two columns usually have different units,
such as dollars and years, so one number cannot be a width in both. gog
therefore refuses `bandwidth` on a contour. It refuses it here too, although
sepal length and petal length are both in centimeters, because the rule counts
the columns, not their units. [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows that
refusal.

`adjust` multiplies the bandwidth gog chooses by itself. It is a plain number
rather than a length, so it means the same thing on either axis. `line`,
`zone`, `surface` and `path` all accept it. The four plots below draw the same
flowers at four values of `adjust`:

```{r}
((data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 0.5) +
    x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("adjust = 0.5: less smooth")) |
   (data(iris_flowers) + path * density +
      x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("default: adjust = 1"))) /
  ((data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 2) +
      x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("adjust = 2: smoother")) |
     (data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 4) +
        x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("adjust = 4: much smoother"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 800)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density adjusted by 0.5, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, beside the same with no adjustment; above the same
adjusted by 2, beside the same adjusted by 4."*

At 0.5 each curve is narrow, so the rings follow small clusters of flowers, and
a few flowers apart from the rest get a small ring of their own. At 1, the
default, the two groups are clear. At 2 the rings around the two groups begin to
merge, and at 4 they form one oval, so the two groups are gone. Too little
smoothing shows every small cluster, and too much hides the groups. Each plot's
legend has its own levels: the smoother the density, the lower its peak.

To estimate one field per category, split the rows with `group`. The level is
already on `color`, which is why the split has to be `group`. Versicolor and
virginica overlap on this plot, while setosa is separate. The `petals` table keeps
only the two that overlap:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(petals)
```

```{r}
data(petals) + path * density(levels = 4) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + group(species) +
  title("two species, estimated separately")
```

*"Given the petals: paths derived by density at 4 levels, x is sepal length, y
is petal length, grouped by species."*

Each species has its own set of rings. Both sets take their colors from the
levels, so the colors do not say which set is which species. Versicolor has the
shorter petals, so its set is the lower one. The two fields
are smoothed alike. On each axis, the two species share the same bandwidth: the
average of the bandwidths each species would get alone. A difference between the
two sets of rings therefore comes from the flowers and not from the smoothing.

### One field, two marks {#one-field-two-marks}

A `zone` given both positions also estimates `density` over both, so it reads
the same field as a path. The difference is in the geometry. A path draws the
rings as strokes. A zone given `levels` fills the bands between them, and
without `levels` it fills small cells. Give both marks the same `levels` and you
get the same curves twice, once as strokes and once as the edges of filled
bands:

```{r}
(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 4) +
   x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("path: the rings")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 4) +
     x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("zone: the bands between them"))
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 4 levels, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, beside zones derived by density at 4 levels, x is
sepal length, y is petal length."*

The left plot draws the four levels as rings. The right plot fills the bands
between the same rings, so the edges of its bands are the rings on the left. A
band is darker where the density is higher. The two legends give the same levels, from
about 0.03 to about 0.13. The filled version is the *filled contour*, and
[`zone * density`](zone.qmd) draws it; the zone chapter covers the color ramp
it uses. One field, two marks. It is [the same division of
work](../grammar.qmd#the-operator-combining) as in `bar * bin` and `line * bin`:
the mark chooses the geometry, and the transform stays the same.

Without `levels`, a zone fills small cells instead of bands, so its color
changes smoothly rather than in steps:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
  title("zone without levels: small cells")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is
petal length."*

Its legend is a continuous ramp of the density, from 0 to about 0.16, rather
than the four levels of the two plots above. Places with almost no flowers get
a pale color too, so the cells fill the panel to its edges.

## A path in polar {#a-path-in-polar}

The arrowhead was the first of the three things the row order gives a path. The
second appears in polar, when the same angle appears in more than one row. Some
routes go around: a compass bearing that turns through all 360 degrees, or a
time of day that starts again at midnight while another value keeps growing. The
`spiral` table holds two days of readings, one every 15 minutes. `a` is the hour
of the day, which goes back to 0 at midnight, and `r` grows the whole time:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(spiral)
```

On flat axes the route has to jump back at midnight:

```{r}
data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) +
  title("a path on flat axes")
```

*"Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r."*

The long stroke across the middle joins 23:45 on the first day to midnight on
the second, and no reading lies along it. On a straight axis the end of one day
is drawn far from the start of the next. On a circle the two are at the same
angle, so the route continues instead of jumping.

`polar()` bends the flat plot into a circle. The `x` value becomes the angle
around the center, and the `y` value becomes the distance from the center.
Here `a` runs from 0 to 23.75, so one day is one full turn, with midnight at
the top. `r` grows from 0.1 to 4, so each reading is a little farther out than
the one before. The same hour on the two days has the same angle, but the second
day's reading is farther from the center, on the second turn.
[Polar](../polar.qmd) teaches the space in full. `path` works in polar like every
other mark:

```{r}
data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a path in polar")
```

*"Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r, in polar."*

The route goes around twice, one day after the other, and turns outward in a
spiral. A `line` cannot draw this. It sorts the rows by `a`, so each moment of
the first day is joined to the same moment of the second, and the stroke
zigzags between them inside one turn:

```{r}
data(spiral) + line + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a line in polar")
```

*"Given the spiral: a line, x is a, y is r, in polar."*

A **segment** is one straight piece of a stroke, between two of its points. One
segment is drawn by `line` but not by `path`: the one that closes a radar chart,
a profile drawn around a circle as in
[Line](line.qmd#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile). The `continents_2007`
table holds one row for each continent, with the mean GDP per person of its
countries:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(continents_2007)
```

```{r}
((data(continents_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(mean_gdp) + polar() +
    title("line: closed")) |
   (data(continents_2007) + path + x(continent) + y(mean_gdp) + polar() +
      title("path: left open"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 460)
```

*"Given continents 2007: a line, x is continent, y is mean gdp, in polar, beside
the same with a path."*

Both plots put each continent on its own spoke. The line joins the last
continent, Oceania, back to the first, Asia. The continents fill the whole turn,
and without that segment one sector of the circle would be left open. The path
leaves that segment out. Its last vertex is where the data stopped, so closing
the route would add a segment that is not in the table. If a route does return
to its start, repeat the first row at the end of the table.

## A path in the cube {#a-path-in-the-cube}

In polar the path still joined the same rows in the same order. A third axis
does not change that either, because the row order does not depend on any axis.
A glider's route has three positions: east, north and altitude. A flat page
holds only two of them. Drawn flat, two circling gliders are two rings, one
inside the other, and nothing on the page shows that they are rising. The
`thermals` table holds one row for each recorded position of two gliders. Both
circle the same thermal, a rising column of warm air, as they climb. The table
is made up for this example: `east` and `north` are meters from the thermal's
center, and `altitude` is the height in meters. A real flight recorder stores
latitude and longitude, which you would convert to meters first:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(thermals)
```

Bind `z` and the route runs through the cube instead of across the page. Of
the marks that join their rows into one stroke, `path` is the only one that
takes `z`, the third position. The reason is the row order this whole chapter is
about:

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")
```

*"Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
glider, with arrow end."*

At every viewing angle, each route joins its rows in the table's order. Its head
marks the glider's last recorded position, at the top of its
climb. A `line` sorts by `x`, and the cube has no left to right. In the
cube `x` is one of three equal positions. At some viewing angles `x` points
straight into the page, so a line would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot
see. So a line's sort by `x` has no meaning in the cube, and `line`, `step`,
`area` and `ribbon` refuse `z` rather than draw a stroke the reader cannot read:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(thermals) + line + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude)
```

Where the two routes cross, the one nearer to you covers the other: at some
crossings Alpha's route is in front, and at others Bravo's. gog draws the short
segments of both routes from the farthest to the nearest, so this stays right at
every angle. That drawing order is the **depth sort**.

As on a flat line, `color` can vary along the route, because a color belongs to
one place on the stroke rather than to the whole stroke. Bind altitude to
`color` as well as to `z`.
The climb is then said twice: once by where the route is, once by what color it
is:

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(altitude) + group(glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Altitude, said twice")
```

*"Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
altitude, grouped by glider, with the viridis palette."*

`palette("viridis")` chooses the color ramp that shows the altitudes.
`space(turn = -25, tilt = 20)` sets the viewing angle, which
[Space](../space.qmd#the-viewing-angle) explains; a `z` binding alone would draw
the cube from its default angle. `group(glider)` tells gog that the rows belong
to two routes rather than one. A *category* on `color` splits the mark into one
stroke per group, but altitude is a *measure* and has no categories to split on.
Remove `group(glider)`, and gog draws a single route with no message, joining
the last row of one glider to the first row of the other with one straight
segment:

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(altitude) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Without group(glider): one route, joined")
```

*"Given the thermals: a path, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
altitude, with the viridis palette."*

That segment cuts down through the cube, from the top of Alpha's
climb to where Bravo's climb starts. `color` shows a value along the route;
`group` says which route each row belongs to. They are two different questions,
so they need two atoms.

A route in the cube can be dashed, as on the flat page:

```{r}
data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20)
```

*"Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by
glider, with pattern dashed."*

[Space](../space.qmd) explains the third dimension and the viewing angle.

## What a path is for {#what-a-path-is-for}

In the three spaces this chapter used (the flat plane, polar and the cube), the
path did one thing: it joined the rows in the table's order. The connected
scatterplot is the best known use, but the mark is more general than that. A
path is the right mark whenever the reader should follow the rows in the order
the table gives them. A route through space is one, as the gliders showed, and
so is an arrow, as the note on Botswana showed. The
test is always the same question. Does the order of the rows mean something? If
it does, the mark is `path`; if the reader should read left to right, it is
`line`.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a path takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("path")
```

The plots below show the two transforms a path takes. Each one returns its new
rows in an order that means something. The path joins them in that order, as
[Two transforms, and the rest refused](#two-transforms-and-the-rest-refused)
explains.

**Counting.** Of the four counting transforms, a path takes only `density`, and
only with a number on both `x` and `y`. `density` then estimates how closely the
rows lie at each place on the plane, one value at each place. The path draws the
rings on which that value is the same. Here the two numbers are the length and
the width of each flower's sepal, from the `iris_flowers` table shown in [The
contour](#the-contour-path-density):

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + path * density + x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) +
  title("path * density")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density, x is sepal length, y is
sepal width."*

The rings mark two crowded places. Setosa's short, wide sepals make the small
group at the left, and the other two species share the larger one.

**Layouts.** `cluster` joins the closest categories into a tree, and the path
draws that tree. It needs a column of values, a second column after `over =`
that names what each value measures, and the categories on one axis, which
become the leaves of the tree. `cluster` returns the rows in the order the tree
is traced. The `nutrients` table holds one row for each pair of food and
nutrient:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(nutrients)
```

```{r}
data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  title("path * cluster")
```

*"Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is
food."*

Each food is described by its `amount` of the five nutrients, and the foods
with the closest amounts join first. `cluster` writes a column, `distance`, and
the `y` axis shows it under the name Distance. The height at which two branches join is how
far apart their amounts are. Beans
and lentils join lowest, so they are the two most alike, and almonds join the
rest at the top. [Cluster](../cluster.qmd) explains how the tree is built.

A path refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. [Two transforms, and
the rest refused](#two-transforms-and-the-rest-refused) gives the reason, using
the summaries: the new rows have no order of their own for a path to follow.
[`line`](line.qmd) draws the counts, the summaries, the fitted lines and the
running total, joined from left to right. [`interval`](interval.qmd) and
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) draw the pairs. The collision modifiers move marks that
would be drawn on top of one another, such as [`point`](point.qmd),
[`bar`](bar.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd). `partition` is drawn by
[`zone`](zone.qmd) and `flow` by [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd). `layout` places a
network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and [`edge`](edge.qmd)
draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A plain stroke does not show which way the route runs. `arrow` adds a head that
shows it. The head belongs to the whole route, not to any one row, so `arrow` is
set in `style()` rather than mapped from a column. A path's `size`, its width,
and its `opacity` are set too, because a path takes one of each for the whole
layer. Each mark takes
its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a path's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("path")
```

`arrow` belongs to `path` and [`edge`](edge.qmd) only, for the reason [Which
end is the last row?](#which-end-is-the-last-row) gave.

A route can take the heads, a width and a stroke pattern together. The plot uses the
`gapminder_asia` table, shown at
[the start of this chapter](#title-block-header):

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow
both, size 2.5 and pattern dotted."*

`arrow` takes a *value* rather than a true-or-false flag. `"both"` is an
ordinary thing to ask for, and a flag would have needed a second setting to say
it. The heads are drawn solid on a dotted path. The dots are the route's texture,
and a head cut into dots no longer reads as an arrow.

This chapter covers the parameters of one transform, `density`: `levels`,
`bandwidth` and `adjust`, in [The parameters](#the-parameters). Its fourth,
`places`, sets the number of places along each axis where the field is computed:
64 by default, which makes a grid of 64 × 64 places. [How many
places](../transforms.qmd#how-many-places-places) covers it.
[Cluster](../cluster.qmd) covers those of `cluster`. Every other property of a
path is either mapped to a column or set with `style()`.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

You might want the route to thicken as income rises, so that the stroke itself
shows a third measure. A mapped `color` can change along a path, one color for
each segment, and a width could change along it in the same way. gog does not
do that: a path takes one size and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per
row. That is the first refusal: mapping `gdp` to `size` is refused:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(gdp)
```

Mapping the same column to `opacity` is refused for the same reason:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)
```

Set either one instead and every segment takes the same width or opacity, which
is the [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) distinction again.

A summary is the second refusal. A path draws the rows in their order, and a
summary replaces those rows, as [Two transforms, and the rest
refused](#two-transforms-and-the-rest-refused) explained:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + path * mean + x(country) + y(life)
```

`density(bandwidth = )` is the third. It is a width in one column's own units,
and the two columns of a contour are usually in different units, so one number
cannot be a width in both:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + path * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length)
```

A path also needs at least two positions in each series (two rows that one
stroke joins), as a line does. Group `gapminder_2007` by country, and each
series holds one row, so nothing would be drawn and gog refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + group(country)
```

## In short {#in-short}

A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them, so sorting the table
changes the picture. That order is the mark's meaning. The arrowhead belongs to
`path` and `edge` only, and the two transforms a path takes are `density` and
`cluster`.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A path takes both positions from every row. [Rule](rule.qmd) draws a different
kind of stroke: it reads one position from each row and draws a stroke across
the whole panel at that value.
